Recommendation: **Definitive diagnosis must be achieved through tissue sampling/excision.** A pre-treatment biopsy of the primary lesion is required, especially when malignancy is not clinically obvious or when non-surgical treatment (e.g., topical agents, laser, radiotherapy) is planned.
**A thorough physical examination of the primary lesion is required** to assess and record its size, location, morphology, and involvement of adjacent structures like the corporal body or urethra.

**A physical examination of both groins must be performed to palpate for lymphadenopathy.** The number, laterality, and characteristics (e.g., mobile, fixed) of any palpable or suspicious inguinal nodes should be recorded.
**Perform magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or penile ultrasound (US) of the primary tumor** when there is uncertainty regarding corporal invasion (T3) and/or the feasibility of organ-sparing surgery.
**Computerized tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis is performed to evaluate for distant metastatic spread.** For high-risk or node-positive disease, ¹⁸F-FDG-PET/CT can also be used.
Cross-sectional imaging (CT, PET/CT) for primary staging should generally be reserved for T3/T4 tumors or in cases of positive lymph node status.
For superficial, non-invasive penile carcinomas (Carcinoma in situ), a fluorescence-diagnostic technique can be used to better determine the extent of the lesion.
**For clinically node-negative (cN0) low-risk tumors (PeIN, pTa, pT1a G1), surveillance of the inguinal lymph nodes is recommended** instead of operative staging.

For clinically node-negative (cN0) intermediate-risk tumors (T1a G2), surveillance may be discussed as an alternative to surgical staging with patients who are willing to comply with strict follow-up.
**For clinically node-negative (cN0) intermediate/high-risk tumors (≥pT1b, or high grade), invasive surgical lymph node staging is recommended.**

**The preferred method for surgical staging in cN0 patients is dynamic sentinel node biopsy (DSNB).** If DSNB is unavailable or not feasible, modified inguinal lymph node dissection (ILND) is an alternative. If DSNB is positive, a completion ILND is recommended.
If DSNB is planned, perform inguinal ultrasound (US) first, with fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of any sonographically abnormal lymph nodes.
In cN0 patients undergoing staging, frozen section analysis should not be performed on tissue from a modified inguinal lymphadenectomy or DSNB.
**For clinically node-positive (cN+) disease, an (image-guided) biopsy of the suspicious node is required to confirm metastasis before initiating treatment.**
**Patients with early-stage, low-grade, and non-invasive tumors should be offered organ- and function-preserving therapy,** depending on the tumor stage and differentiation grade.

**The goal of surgical treatment is complete excision with negative margins (R0).** A margin of 5 mm for G1/G2 tumors and 10 mm for G3 tumors is suggested. In case of a positive surgical margin, a re-excision should be performed.

**Offer patients a balanced and individualized discussion on the benefits and harms of possible treatment options.** Inform them of the higher risk of local recurrence when using organ-sparing treatments compared to amputative surgery.

**Topical therapy with 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) or imiquimod can be offered to patients with biopsy-confirmed superficial disease (PeIN/Tis, Ta).** Patients should be informed about limited efficacy and potential off-label use.
**If topical treatment fails, it should not be repeated.**

Example regimens for topical therapy include:
• **Imiquimod 5% cream:** Apply at night three times per week for 4–16 weeks.
• **5-FU cream 5%:** Apply twice daily for 2–6 weeks.
Topical therapy is ineffective for more advanced stages of penile cancer.
**Laser ablation (e.g., CO₂ or Nd:YAG laser) can be used for biopsy-confirmed superficial or early-stage tumors (PeIN/Tis, Ta, T1).**
A surgical margin of 5 mm is considered oncologically safe for laser therapy.
**After topical or laser therapy, a control biopsy should be performed to verify local tumor control,** especially in cases of clinical doubt.

**Organ-sparing surgery options (circumcision, wide local excision, glansectomy, Mohs) are offered for lesions confined to the glans and prepuce (PeIN, Ta, T1-T2)** in patients willing to comply with strict follow-up.
**Intra-operative frozen section analysis of resection margins should be performed** to confirm negative margins, especially in cases of doubt.
**Circumcision can be a curative treatment for tumors confined to the prepuce (PeIN/Tis, Ta).**
When using radiotherapy or topical therapy for a preputial lesion, a circumcision should be performed first.
**Wide local excision (WLE) is an option for early-stage tumors (PeIN, Ta, T1).** Complete excision with wide negative margins is required.

**Mohs micrographic surgery can be considered as an alternative to WLE for select, low-grade, superficial lesions,** particularly on the glans or distal penis, if the appropriate expertise is available.
**Glansectomy (partial or total) or glans resurfacing are options for tumors located on the glans penis (PeIN, Ta, T1-T2).** Reconstruction may be performed with a split-thickness skin graft.

**Partial or total penectomy is recommended for patients with higher stage tumors (T2, T3, T4), particularly with invasion of the corpora cavernosa,** unfavorable histopathology, or for those not suitable for organ-sparing approaches.

**Radiotherapy (often brachytherapy) can be an alternative to surgery for selected patients with T1-T2 tumors (<4 cm),** particularly those who are unfit for surgery. Patients should be informed of a potentially lower local control rate compared to surgery.
For T3–4 or N+ surgically unresectable disease, consider EBRT with concurrent chemotherapy to the penis and regional lymph nodes.

Specific radiotherapy doses may include:
• **EBRT:** 66-74 Gy in 2 Gy fractions.
• **Brachytherapy (HDR):** 42-45 Gy in 12-14 fractions.
• **Brachytherapy (LDR/PDR):** 60-65 Gy delivered continuously over ~5 days.
For non-resectable, locally advanced primary tumors (T4), consider induction/neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgery for responders, or chemo-radiotherapy.

**Local recurrence after organ-sparing surgery should be treated according to the principles of primary tumor management.** Small, non-invasive recurrences can be treated with salvage organ-sparing options.
For large local recurrences or those with invasion of the corpora cavernosa, partial or total penectomy is warranted.
After radiotherapy, local recurrence should be treated with surgical salvage therapy.
After topical or laser therapy, local recurrence should be treated with a different treatment modality.
Regional lymph node recurrence after initial surveillance should be managed according to the same principles as primary lymph node metastases (i.e., with ILND +/- systemic therapy).
Regional lymph node recurrence after a prior radical lymphadenectomy should be managed with a multimodal approach, including neoadjuvant chemotherapy, surgery, and/or radiotherapy.
Following circumcision for a primary tumor, patients with moderately or poorly differentiated tumors (grades 2 and 3) will require inguinal node dissection.

For palpable, mobile inguinal nodes (cN1-cN2), inguinal lymph node dissection (ILND) is recommended. The dissection may be fascial-sparing or radical, with preservation of the saphenous vein where possible.

If intraoperatively suspicious nodes are removed during surgery for cN+ disease, frozen section analysis should be performed. If positive, an ipsilateral radical lymphadenectomy should be completed in the same session.
**For bulky, fixed, or extensive inguinal nodes (cN3), neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) with a cisplatin- and taxane-based regimen is preferred over up-front surgery.**
Minimally-invasive ILND for cN1–2 disease should only be offered as part of a clinical trial. It is contraindicated for cN3 disease.
**Following a response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, patients should undergo consolidative surgery,** including radical inguinal lymphadenectomy and possible pelvic lymphadenectomy.
**Ipsilateral pelvic lymph node dissection (PLND) is recommended for patients with ≥2-3 positive inguinal nodes on one side or with extranodal extension.**
**Recommended neoadjuvant chemotherapy regimens are cisplatin- and taxane-based triplets,** such as TIP (Paclitaxel/Ifosfamide/Cisplatin) or TPF (Cisplatin/Paclitaxel/5-Fluorouracil).
**Adjuvant chemotherapy should be considered for patients with pN2 or pN3 disease** following lymph node dissection.
Adjuvant radiotherapy (with or without chemo-sensitization) should be offered or considered for patients with high-risk pathological findings such as pN2/N3 disease or extranodal extension.
Definitive radiotherapy (with or without chemo sensitization) can be offered to patients who are unwilling or unable to undergo surgery.
**For first-line treatment of metastatic disease, platinum-based combination chemotherapy is the preferred approach.** Recommended regimens include TIP, TPF, or cisplatin + 5-FU.
**Bleomycin-containing chemotherapy regimens should not be used** due to the risk of pulmonary toxicity.
For patients with progressive disease, enrollment in a clinical trial is the preferred option for subsequent-line therapy.
Subsequent-line therapy options may include paclitaxel monotherapy or, for biomarker-selected tumors (MSI-H, dMMR, TMB-H), immunotherapy such as pembrolizumab.
Patients with metastatic disease or requiring multimodal therapy should be discussed in an interdisciplinary tumor board.
Palliative radiotherapy can be offered for symptom control in advanced disease (e.g., 30 Gy in 10 fractions).
For chronic lymphedema resulting from treatment, a complex decongestive therapy (lymphatic drainage, compression therapy, and skin care) should be performed.
**Close, regular, and risk-stratified follow-up is crucial after treatment,** especially for the first 2-5 years, to detect recurrences and functional disorders.
A general follow-up schedule is every 3-4 months for the first 2 years, then less frequently. Follow-up should extend for at least 5 years.

Specific follow-up schedules after laser therapy are:
• **CO2 Laser:** After 2 months, then every 3 months for 3 years, then biannually.
• **Nd:YAG Laser:** Every 3 months for 2 years, then biannually.

Specific follow-up schedules based on treatment:
• **Organ Preservation:** Every 3 mo (Yrs 1-2), every 6 mo (Yrs 3-5).
• **Total Penectomy:** Every 3 mo (Yrs 1-2), annually (Yrs 3-5).
**Patients should be taught self-examination** for early detection of recurrence and given easy access back to the clinic if concerns arise.
Penile cancer care should be delivered by an extended multi-disciplinary team including specialists in urology, oncology, nursing, pathology, radiology, psychology, and lymphedema therapy.
**Patients should be offered psychological support and counseling,** and physicians should discuss the psychological and functional (urinary, sexual) impact of the disease and its treatments.
Patients should be assessed for lymphedema at follow-up and referred to lymphedema therapists early if it develops.
